derived_from: three independent open codings (A, B, C) over the same 45-file stratified packet
unit_of_analysis: one heading section, or one ~1500-char slice of an oversized/headingless section
rule: assign by the job the block does for the coding agent, never by its heading text

categories.definition: Gives the agent a mental model of what this project is, how it is structured, and where things live, so it can navigate without exploring.
includes: what the project does, who it is for, its domain vocabulary
directory/module maps, package layouts, monorepo topology
architecture descriptions, data/control flow, component responsibilities
tech stack and dependency inventories presented as facts to know
excludes: a rule the code must satisfy -> project-invariants
a pointer telling the agent to go read another file -> context-routing
a command to run -> command-recipes
discriminators: Is this describing what EXISTS, or prescribing what the agent must DO or SATISFY? Description -> here.

categories.definition: Supplies the exact invocations the agent should run — build, test, lint, run, generate, deploy — so it does not guess or invent commands.
includes: copy-pasteable shell commands and their flags
how to run a single test vs the whole suite
package-manager, task-runner and script tables
tool invocation syntax specific to this repo
excludes: when the command must be run to call work finished -> completion-gates
an ordered multi-step method for a task class -> task-procedure
a ban on running something -> hard-boundaries
discriminators: Strip the surrounding prose: is the payload a literal invocation the agent would execute? Yes -> here.
A command listed as a required exit check belongs to completion-gates, not here.

categories.definition: Fixes the surface form of whatever the agent writes — code, tests, comments, documentation, commit text — so its output is indistinguishable from the project's existing work.
includes: naming, formatting, indentation, import order, language idioms
typing/annotation conventions, comment and docstring style
file placement and naming patterns for new files
wording and structure conventions for prose the agent writes
excludes: the mechanics/policy of submitting the change -> contribution-protocol
a semantic contract that makes code correct rather than consistent -> project-invariants
the command that reformats the code -> command-recipes
discriminators: If the agent violated this, would the result be WRONG or merely INCONSISTENT? Inconsistent -> here; wrong -> project-invariants.

categories.definition: States semantic contracts that must hold in this codebase — rules that generic engineering knowledge would violate, where breaking them produces something broken, unsafe, or silently wrong.
includes: always route through wrapper X, never call Y directly
this field/table/state is authoritative; never derive or duplicate it
required error-handling, concurrency, migration or security contracts
framework- or repo-specific correctness rules a competent outsider would get wrong
excludes: a ban on an ACTION the agent takes -> hard-boundaries
a cosmetic/consistency preference -> house-form
'when you change X also change Y' -> cochange-duties
discriminators: Is the constraint about a property the CODE must hold, or about an action the AGENT must not take? Code property -> here.

categories.definition: Removes options from the agent's action space outright: things it must never do, touch, or run, with no conditional path back.
includes: never force-push / never rewrite history / never touch main
never edit these files or directories
never run destructive, irreversible or production-affecting commands
never commit secrets, never disable tests to make them pass
excludes: stop and ask a human first -> human-authority
a property the code must satisfy -> project-invariants
a check that must pass before done -> completion-gates
discriminators: Is there ANY path where the agent may proceed? If it must ask first -> human-authority. If never -> here.

categories.definition: Defines the exit bar: what must be run and what evidence must exist before the agent may call work done, commit, or hand back.
includes: run these checks before committing / before claiming done
required test, lint, typecheck, build gates and their pass criteria
definition-of-done checklists and required evidence
'never report success without X'
excludes: the command itself, listed as a capability -> command-recipes
the order of work steps -> task-procedure
who approves the result -> human-authority
discriminators: Does this block gate the CLAIM of completion? If it only tells you how to invoke something, it is command-recipes.

categories.definition: Prescribes the ordered method for a class of task — the sequence of steps to follow when doing a kind of work in this repo.
includes: how to add a feature / fix a bug / add an endpoint, step by step
TDD or plan-first workflows mandated for this repo
branch-and-work sequences, migration procedures, release runbooks
'first do A, then B, only then C'
excludes: how the agent should think, talk, or delegate -> agent-conduct
the checks that end the work -> completion-gates
the literal commands used inside the steps -> command-recipes
discriminators: Is there an ORDER being imposed on task work? Yes -> here. If it configures the agent rather than the task -> agent-conduct.

categories.definition: Configures the agent as an actor rather than the codebase: how it reasons, how much it plans or delegates, how verbose or autonomous it is, what tone and response shape it uses, and how it weighs open-ended tradeoffs.
includes: reasoning depth, planning before acting, self-verification habits
response length, tone, language, formatting of replies to the human
subagent/parallelism/tool-use policy
engineering value orderings used to settle tradeoffs (simplicity over cleverness, etc.)
persona or role definitions for the agent
excludes: an ordered procedure for a task -> task-procedure
when to hand control to a person -> human-authority
the form of code/commits it writes -> house-form
discriminators: Would this block still make sense in a different repo? Agent-configuration usually would; repo rules would not.

categories.definition: Routes the agent to the right resource at the right moment: which deeper document, rule file, skill, slash command, or MCP tool to load or use, and under what condition.
includes: 'for X, read docs/Y.md'
@-includes, nested AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md precedence rules
inventories of installed skills, slash commands, MCP servers and when to reach for them
conditional dispatch tables mapping situations to resources
excludes: the content itself, inlined -> whichever category the content serves
a shell command to execute -> command-recipes
discriminators: Does the block's value lie in POINTING somewhere else rather than in its own content? Yes -> here.

categories.definition: Pre-loads hard-won empirical knowledge about how this environment actually behaves — known failure modes, misleading signals, surprising defaults — so the agent does not rediscover or misdiagnose them.
includes: 'X looks broken but is actually Y'
known-flaky tests, misleading error messages, stale caches
environment/platform quirks, version traps, tooling gotchas
symptom-keyed corrective notes
excludes: a flat prohibition with no diagnostic content -> hard-boundaries
a correctness contract of the codebase -> project-invariants
discriminators: Does the block explain a SURPRISE — something that would mislead a competent agent? Yes -> here.

categories.definition: Binds artifacts together: when the agent changes X it must also update Y in the same change, so paired state does not drift.
includes: change the schema -> regenerate types / write a migration
add a flag -> update docs, README, changelog, tests
edit source -> update the corresponding snapshot or fixture
excludes: a required check before done -> completion-gates
a general correctness contract -> project-invariants
discriminators: Is the trigger 'you edited a specific artifact'? Yes -> here.

categories.definition: Marks where the agent must stop and hand control to a person: which actions need approval, when to ask instead of assume, and how the agent and its human coordinate live.
includes: ask before installing dependencies / changing architecture / deleting data
'when uncertain, ask rather than guess'
approval checkpoints, escalation rules, how to present options for a decision
what the agent must report back and when
excludes: an unconditional ban -> hard-boundaries
reply tone/verbosity in normal operation -> agent-conduct
discriminators: Does a HUMAN decision unblock the agent here? Yes -> here.

categories.definition: Governs how the agent's work enters the project: the mechanics and the policy of submitting a change so the project's humans will accept it.
includes: branch naming, commit message format, conventional-commit types, DCO/sign-off
PR templates, required descriptions, review and CI expectations
duplicate-work checks before opening a PR, issue-claiming etiquette
rules about whether and how AI-generated contributions are accepted, disclosure requirements
excludes: the writing style of the commit text itself -> house-form
the checks that must pass before committing -> completion-gates
the git commands used -> command-recipes
discriminators: Is this about getting the change ACCEPTED by the project's humans/process? Yes -> here.

OTHER.definition: The block does no job for a coding agent, or does a job this codebook has no home for.
typical: end-user product documentation pasted wholesale (API usage examples, benchmarks, license text, sponsorship/community sections)
human-audience advice about supervising AI rather than instructions to the agent
OTHER.requirement: always give a one-line reason naming the purpose you saw

merge_notes: capability-surface (C only, 0.06) folded into context-routing — A and B both defined routing to explicitly include skills and tools.
engineering-values (A only, 0.05) folded into agent-conduct as tradeoff-weighting; if it resurfaces as OTHER in volume, promote it.
ai-contribution-governance (A, 0.03) merged with contribution-protocol (B, 0.06) — one job: get the change accepted by the project's humans.
project-invariants and hard-boundaries kept separate (2/3 support each) — C lumped them, but 'property the code must hold' and 'action the agent must not take' answer different questions.
